{{Short description|Mathematical operation}}
{{Use American English|date = April 2019}}
{{Calculus |Differential}}
[[File:4 fonctions du second degré.svg|right|thumb|200px|The second derivative of a [[quadratic function]] is [[constant function|constant]].]]

In [[calculus]], the '''second derivative''', or the '''second-order derivative''', of a [[function (mathematics)|function]] {{math|''f''}} is the [[derivative]] of the derivative of {{math|''f''}}. Informally, the second derivative can be phrased as "the rate of change of the rate of change"; for example, the second derivative of the position of an object with respect to time is the [[instantaneous acceleration]] of the object, or the rate at which the [[velocity]] of the object is changing with respect to time. In [[Leibniz notation]]:
<math display="block">a =  \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2},</math>
where {{math|''a''}} is acceleration, {{math|''v''}} is velocity, {{mvar|t}} is time, {{math|''x''}} is position, and d is the instantaneous "delta" or change. The last expression <math>\tfrac{d^2 x}{dt^2}</math> is the second derivative of position ({{math|''x''}}) with respect to time.

On the [[graph of a function]], the sign of the second derivative is related to the [[convex function|concavity]] of the graph. The graph of a function with a positive second derivative is upwardly concave, while the graph of a function with a negative second derivative curves in the opposite way.

== Second derivative power rule ==
The [[power rule]] for the first derivative, if applied twice, will produce the second derivative power rule as follows:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2}{dx^2} x^n = \frac{d}{dx}\frac{d}{dx} x^n = \frac{d}{dx} \left(n x^{n-1}\right) = n \frac{d}{dx} x^{n-1} = n(n - 1)x^{n-2}.</math>

== Notation ==
{{Details|Notation for differentiation}}
The second derivative of a function <math>f(x)</math> is usually denoted <math>f''(x)</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Content - The second derivative|url=https://amsi.org.au/ESA_Senior_Years/SeniorTopic3/3b/3b_2content_10.html|access-date=2020-09-16 | website=amsi.org.au}}</ref> That is:
<math display="block">f'' = \left(f'\right)'</math>
When using [[Leibniz's notation]] for derivatives, the second derivative of a dependent variable {{mvar|y}} with respect to an independent variable {{mvar|x}} is written
<math display="block">\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.</math>
This notation is derived from the following formula:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \,=\, \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right).</math>

== Example ==
Given the function
<math display="block">f(x) = x^3,</math>
the derivative of {{math|''f''}} is the function
<math display="block">f'(x) = 3x^2.</math>
The second derivative of {{math|''f''}} is the derivative of <math>f'</math>, namely
<math display="block">f''(x) = 6x.</math>

== Relation to the graph ==
[[File:Animated illustration of inflection point.gif|500px|thumb|A plot of <math>f(x) = \sin(2x)</math> from <math>-\pi/4</math> to <math>5\pi/4</math>. The tangent line is blue where the curve is concave up, green where the curve is concave down, and red at the inflection points (0, <math>\pi</math>/2, and <math>\pi</math>).]]

=== Concavity ===
The second derivative of a function {{math|''f''}} can be used to determine the '''concavity''' of the graph of {{math|''f''}}.  A function whose second derivative is positive is said to be [[concave up]] (also referred to as convex), meaning that the [[tangent line]] near the point where it touches the function will lie below the graph of the function.  Similarly, a function whose second derivative is negative will be [[concave down]] (sometimes simply called concave), and its tangent line will lie above the graph of the function near the point of contact.

=== Inflection points ===
{{main|Inflection point}}
If the second derivative of a function changes sign, the graph of the function will switch from concave down to concave up, or vice versa.  A point where this occurs is called an '''inflection point'''.  Assuming the second derivative is continuous, it must take a value of zero at any inflection point, although not every point where the second derivative is zero is necessarily a point of inflection.

=== Second derivative test ===
{{main|Second derivative test}}
The relation between the second derivative and the graph can be used to test whether a [[stationary point]] for a function (i.e., a point where <math>f'(x) = 0</math>) is a [[local maximum]] or a [[local minimum]].  Specifically,
* If <math>f''(x) < 0</math>, then <math>f</math> has a local maximum at <math>x</math>.
* If <math>f''(x) > 0</math>, then <math>f</math> has a local minimum at <math>x</math>.
* If <math>f''(x) = 0</math>, the second derivative test says nothing about the point <math>x</math>, a possible inflection point.
The reason the second derivative produces these results can be seen by way of a real-world analogy. Consider a vehicle that at first is moving forward at a great velocity, but with a negative acceleration. Clearly, the position of the vehicle at the point where the velocity reaches zero will be the maximum distance from the starting position – after this time, the velocity will become negative and the vehicle will reverse. The same is true for the minimum, with a vehicle that at first has a very negative velocity but positive acceleration.

== Limit ==
It is possible to write a single [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] for the second derivative:
<math display="block">f''(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)}{h^2}.</math>

The limit is called the [[second symmetric derivative]].<ref name="Zygmund2002">{{cite book|author=A. Zygmund |author-link=Antoni Zygmund | title=Trigonometric Series|title-link= Trigonometric Series |year=2002|publisher=Cambridge University Press | isbn=978-0-521-89053-3 | pages=22–23}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | first= Brian S. 
 | last= Thomson 
 | year= 1994 
 | title= Symmetric Properties of Real Functions
 | publisher= Marcel Dekker
 | isbn= 0-8247-9230-0
 | page = 1
}}</ref> The second symmetric derivative may exist even when the (usual) second derivative does not.

The expression on the right can be written as a [[difference quotient]] of difference quotients:
<math display="block">\frac{f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)}{h^2} = \frac{\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} - \dfrac{f(x) - f(x-h)}{h}}{h}.</math>
This limit can be viewed as a continuous version of the [[second difference]] for [[sequence (mathematics)|sequences]].

However, the existence of the above limit does not mean that the function <math>f</math> has a second derivative. The limit above just gives a possibility for calculating the second derivative—but does not provide a definition. A counterexample is the [[sign function]] <math>\sgn(x)</math>, which is defined as:
<math display="block">\sgn(x) = \begin{cases}
-1 & \text{if } x < 0, \\
0 & \text{if } x = 0, \\
1 & \text{if } x > 0.
\end{cases}</math>

The sign function is not continuous at zero, and therefore the second derivative for <math>x = 0</math> does not exist. But the above limit exists for <math>x = 0</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sgn(0+h) - 2\sgn(0) + \sgn(0-h)}{h^2}
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sgn(h) - 2\cdot 0 + \sgn(-h)}{h^2} \\
&= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sgn(h) + (-\sgn(h))}{h^2} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{0}{h^2} = 0.
\end{align}</math>

== Quadratic approximation ==
Just as the first derivative is related to [[linear approximation]]s, the second derivative is related to the best [[quadratic approximation]] for a function {{math|''f''}}.  This is the [[quadratic function]] whose first and second derivatives are the same as those of {{math|''f''}} at a given point. The formula for the best quadratic approximation to a function {{math|''f''}} around the point {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}} is
<math display="block">f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \tfrac{1}{2} f''(a)(x-a)^2.</math>
This quadratic approximation is the second-order [[Taylor polynomial]] for the function centered at {{math|1=''x'' = ''a''}}.

== Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative ==

For many combinations of [[boundary conditions]] explicit formulas for [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative]] can be obtained. For example, assuming <math>x \in [0,L]</math> and homogeneous [[Dirichlet boundary conditions]] (i.e., <math> v(0) = v(L) = 0</math> where {{math|''v''}} is the eigenvector), the [[eigenvalues]] are <math> \lambda_j = -\tfrac{j^2 \pi^2}{L^2}</math> and the corresponding [[eigenvectors]] (also called [[eigenfunctions]]) are {{nowrap|<math> v_j(x) = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{L}} \sin\left(\tfrac{j \pi x}{L}\right) </math>.}} Here, {{nowrap|<math> v''_j(x) = \lambda_j v_j(x)</math>,}} for {{nowrap|<math> j = 1,\ldots,\infty</math>.}}

For other well-known cases, see [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the second derivative]].

== Generalization to higher dimensions ==

=== The Hessian ===
{{main|Hessian matrix}}
The second derivative generalizes to higher dimensions through the notion of second [[partial derivative]]s.  For a function {{math|''f'': '''R'''<sup>3</sup> → '''R'''}}, these include the three second-order partials
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}, \; \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2}, \text{ and }\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}</math>
and the mixed partials
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \, \partial y}, \; \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \, \partial z}, \text{ and } \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \, \partial z}.</math>

If the function's image and domain both have a potential, then these fit together into a [[symmetric matrix]] known as the '''Hessian'''.  The [[eigenvalue]]s of this matrix can be used to implement a multivariable analogue of the second derivative test.  (See also the [[second partial derivative test]].)

=== The Laplacian ===
{{main|Laplace operator}}
Another common generalization of the second derivative is the '''Laplacian'''.  This is the differential operator <math>\nabla^2</math> (or <math>\Delta</math>) defined by
<math display="block">\nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}.</math>
The Laplacian of a function is equal to the [[divergence]] of the [[gradient]], and the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of the [[Hessian matrix]].
